overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 13
overview.pill: Using Different Forms for Quadratic Functions
overview.text: MP.7MP.7Throughout this lesson students look for and make use of the structure of expressions when completing the square. They see algebraic expressions, such as (x-h)^{2}, as single objects and the completed-square form as a single object being composed of several objects. They recognize that the graph has a minimum or maximum point from the standard form of the quadratic equation, and they can use the structure to transform it into its vertex form. Once in that form, they use the structure of the completed-square expression to identify the coordinates of the vertex.
outcomes: Students solve complex quadratic equations, including those with a leading coefficient other than 1, by completing the square. Some solutions may be irrational. Students draw conclusions about the properties of irrational numbers, including closure for the irrational number system under various operations.
overview.teacherInsight: Emphasize precise mathematical definitions and multiple problem-solving representations. Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their numerical solutions.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 13 Exit Ticket: Solving Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
exitTicket.prompt:
Exit Ticket

Solve the following quadratic equation both by factoring and by completing the square: \frac{1}{4}x^{2}-x=3.

Which method do you prefer to solve this equation? Justify your answer using algebraic reasoning.
exitTicket.solution:
Solve the following quadratic equation both by factoring and by completing the square: \frac{1}{4}x^{2}-x=3.

Factoring—you can eliminate the fraction by multiplying both sides by 4 to obtain an equivalent expression. x^{2}-4x=12x^{2}-4x-12=0(x-6)(x+2)=0x=6 or -2

Completing the Square―you can start by either multiplying both sides by 4 or by factoring out \frac{1}{4} as the GCF.

\frac{1}{4}(x^{2}-4x+____)=3\frac{1}{4}(x^{2}-4x+4)=3+1x^{2}-4x+4=16(x-2)^{2}=16x=2±4x=6 or -2

Which method do you prefer to solve this equation? Justify your answer using algebraic reasoning.

Students may have a personal preference about which way is easier; therefore, either answer is correct, but it should have mathematical reasoning to support it. They may prefer factoring since they are more familiar with it or because having a fraction as the leading coefficient can make completing the square trickier. Notice that in the factoring response, the fraction was eliminated in the first step. Remind students that this is often an option to make an equation look friendlier.
